## Blog articles (full text)

### Speed Up Your Shopify Theme: Liquid Tips that Move CRO Needles
https://muhammad.dev/blog/shopify-theme-speed.html

Most Shopify stores leave a 5–15% conversion lift on the table because the theme loads slower than it should. Europeans and mobile shoppers are the hardest hit, and no amount of discounting fixes a storefront that feels sluggish. Here is the playbook Muhammad uses when he optimizes a theme.

**Measure before you touch Liquid.** The fastest "speed fix" is usually nothing to write code for. Open the theme editor, audit third-party apps, and check asset variants in the merchant admin. Apps injected onto every page are the single biggest hidden weight in modern themes — removing one render-blocking script often beats a week of refactoring.

**Trim Liquid at the template level.** Liquid runs server-side on every request, so heavy loops and stale conditions cost real milliseconds on the first paint. The wins that matter:
- Replace expensive `for` loops with `limit` and `offset` so you only render what the design shows.
- Lazily load below-the-fold sections and use `loading="lazy"` on images.
- Inline only critical CSS and move the rest into a deferred stylesheet.
- Ship product images in `img_url: '800x'` sized to the container, with WebP generated by Shopify's image pipeline.

**Core Web Vitals as a conversion lever.** Google and shoppers agree: LCP under 2.5 seconds and CLS near zero feel "fast". For product pages the highest-leverage fixes are usually the hero image, a stable layout for the add-to-cart section, and deferring the recommendation scripts that cause layout shift.

**What this means for a storeowner.** You don't need a full rebuild to get fast. Profile first, cut app bloat second, then make targeted Liquid and asset changes. On a recent client store this sequence took LCP from ~4.1s to ~1.9s and lifted conversion noticeably — without changing the design at all.

Bottom line: Speed is a conversion lever most stores ignore. Profile the theme, cut app and Liquid weight, then make targeted asset changes — a full rebuild is usually unnecessary.

### Next.js SEO in 2026: Metadata, Core Web Vitals, and GEO
https://muhammad.dev/blog/nextjs-seo.html

SEO in 2026 isn't only about ranking in Google — it's about being understandable to both search engines and AI agents. Next.js gives the tools for both, but only if used deliberately. This is the checklist Muhammad applies to every Next.js site he ships.

**Metadata is the foundation.** Use the App Router's `export const metadata` per page rather than a single global config. Every route should own its title, description, canonical, and Open Graph tags. For dynamic pages, generate metadata from the route's data — a product page whose title literally names the product outperforms a generic template title every time.

**Rendering strategy matters.** Static generation where possible, server rendering where data is fresh, and dynamic only where truly needed. Most marketing and blog pages should be static or ISR so the HTML is fast and cacheable. Content that never changes should never block the first paint behind a client-side fetch.

**Core Web Vitals are an SEO input.** LCP, INP, and CLS feed directly into how search engines treat pages. For Next.js that means:
- Use the `next/image` component — it sets `loading="lazy"`, responsive sizes, and proper priority hints.
- Ship fonts with `next/font` to avoid render-blocking font swaps.
- Keep interactive scripts deferred with `next/script` strategy="afterInteractive".
- Validate with Lighthouse and field data from PageSpeed Insights, not just dev tools.

**GEO: visibility to generative engines.** AI assistants increasingly answer questions by citing pages they can parse reliably. Clear headings, concise summaries at the top of the page, semantic HTML, and structured data (FAQ, Product, Article schema) all make content easier for a model to quote — and easier to cite the brand when it does.

Bottom line: Rankings are no longer a single dashboard. Treat speed, semantics, and structure as one system. Per-route metadata, static-first rendering, and quotable structure cover both human and AI search.

### Your Website is Invisible to AI Agents. Fix That First.
https://muhammad.dev/blog/agentic-web.html

When someone asks an AI assistant "what's the best way to buy X", the assistant doesn't browse a site for joy — it reads it so it can quote and cite it. If pages are hard to parse, you win nothing, even when you'd have ranked in the old search results.

**Two audiences, one page.** A website now needs to answer for two readers at once: humans who skim, and models that extract. The good news is the same fixes serve both. Clear structure, honest claims, and scannable answers satisfy a real visitor and make an agent confident enough to recommend your page.

**The practical checklist:**
- Lead each page with a one-sentence summary — the most quotable sentence is the first one.
- Use real heading hierarchy (one H1, logical H2s) instead of styled divs.
- Add structured data: `Product`, `FAQ`, and `Article` schema cost nothing and make facts explicit.
- Write plain, specific numbers and claims — "trusted by 5,000+ travelers" beats vague marketing.
- Keep key pages server-rendered and indexable; don't hide content behind client-side-only renders.

**Why this is a business decision.** Research habits are shifting faster than most marketing funnels are updating for them. Treating "AI visibility" as part of your SEO budget isn't a trend-chase — it's insurance that your brand stays quotable as discovery keeps moving off the classic search result page.

Bottom line: A growing share of product research happens inside AI agents, not search engines. Lead with a one-sentence summary, real heading hierarchy, structured data, and specific, quotable claims.
